item.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
item.description:
NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision.
Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027.
Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight.
“As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!”
Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using bothradioisotopeand fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable.
Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space.
NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineerswebsite.
The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.Future Engineersadministers the challenge through a contract with theNASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovationwithin the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

item.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
item.description:
On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation.
Since 2012, NASASpace Apps Challengehas hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries. The challenge provides an opportunity for hands-on experience with NASA science, mobilizing an engaged global community of technologists and space science enthusiasts to answer questions that benefit humanity and drive exploration.
Participants join events organized by local volunteers to work in teams and address one of the challenges and submit their project before the deadline. Projects are then judged to determine 10 global winners, to be announced in January.
“The Space Apps Challenge invites people with many different skillsets to leverage NASA’s gold-standard datasets to address real challenges facing us here on Earth and in space,” said Amy Kaminski, engagement branch chief, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We’re thrilled to see more than 180,000 people tackling these challenges and helping to accelerate our ability to find solutions.”
Challenges also feature data from 17 international space agency partners, all Artemis Accord signatories. This year’s space agency partners are: Angola National Space Programme Management Office (GGPEN), Bahrain Space Agency, Brazilian Space Agency (AEB), CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation), Italian Space Agency, JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Center of the United Arab Emirates, National Space Activities Commission of Argentina (CONAE), Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, Paraguayan Space Agency, Senegalese Space Studies Agency, Spanish Space Agency, Turkish Space Agency, and UK Space Agency. Three agencies, GGPEN, AEB, and CONAE, also wrote challenges this year.

item.title: BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge
item.description:
The NASA Space Biology Program within theBiological and Physical Sciences(BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep space missions, the need to protect individual crew members with personalized, data-driven health strategies is becoming increasingly important.
The originalAVATAR(A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation, which flew aboard the Artemis II mission, marks a significant milestone: organ-on-a-chip devices constructed from the cells of actual crew members returned from a 10-day lunar flyby on April 10, 2026. AVATAR is the first demonstration of an Artemis astronaut analog using an organ-on-a-chip model to generate personalized biological insights that can inform medical kits and countermeasures for future deep space missions.
Digital twins represent a key strategy for addressing these challenges. By developing individualized computational physiological models that can be iteratively refined with empirical data, these frameworks integrate environmental, physiological, and multi-omics inputs. This approach allows for the simulation and prediction of how a specific individual will respond to spaceflight stressors.
The BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge invites the scientific community to apply innovative computational digital twin technologies to accelerate biological discovery, biochemical and molecular modeling, and predictions of individual astronaut health outcomes. The digital twin will be a computational model of how the AVATAR bone marrow chip responds to spaceflight stressors.
The proposed digital twin frameworks must be capable of processing diverse multi-modal datasets and leverage established computational biology methods alongside modern digital twin architectures to create personalized, predictive models of astronaut physiology. These systems are expected to model each astronaut’s immune and bone marrow hematopoietic responses to spaceflight, integrating multi-modal data to generate tailored health predictions — including comparative analysis that distinguishes individual-specific effects from effects common across the crew. Proposals should also demonstrate a pathway to continuous model updating as new empirical data become available, reflecting the iterative nature of a true digital twin.
For more information including registration,rules, and eligibility, visit:https://work.crowdplat.com/challenge/bps-digital-twin-challenge

item.title: New Album of Baby Star Sounds Shared by NASA’s Chandra
item.description:
A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound.
Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and young stars are present, astronomers can better understand the lifecycle of all stars, including our own Sun.
The galaxy Messier 82 (M82) is called a starburst galaxy because stars are forming there at a rate tens or even hundreds of times higher than in our Milky Way galaxy. This stellar birth boom may be due to a collision with another galaxy in the past. Today, Chandra sees giant plumes of hot gas that are the byproduct of young, giant stars that quickly explode and other star formation activity. One of the new sonifications combines Chandra’s data with optical data from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, as well as infrared views from NASA’s James Webb and retired Spitzer space telescopes. The sonification of the three types of light begins with a radar-like scan that is louder where sources are brighter. The X-ray data is mapped to the highest range of frequencies heard. Infrared data is heard as a low drone plus plucked sounds, while the optical data turns into a range of musical pitches and textures.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser thatsupports HTML5 video
One of the closest and busiest star formation regions to Earth is the Orion Nebula (visible just below the belt in the Orion constellation with a small telescope and dark skies). Chandra sees more than a thousand stars in this area that are very energetic and active in their infancy. In the sonified version of the Chandra data, these stars are twinkling sounds, while the diffuse X-ray emission is mapped to pure high tones. An infrared image from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the raw material of dust and gas used to build these new stars, and its data is heard as lower musical tones, distorted string instruments, and a digital harp.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser thatsupports HTML5 video
A portion of the Carina Nebula, another star formation region, is nicknamed the “Cosmic Cliffs” because of its spectacular structure seen in infrared by NASA’s Webb. Chandra also looks at this region, seeing through the dust and gas, and detects individual baby stars – which are turned into short string sounds in the sonification. A diffuse X-ray glow throughout the region has longer strings notes assigned to it. The nebula in the Webb data is mapped to a sustained sound, punctuated by other instruments to denote features like stars and ridges.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser thatsupports HTML5 video
Rho Ophiuchi is a striking star-forming cloud, filled with gas and stars of different sizes and ages. Chandra reveals infant stars that violently flare and produce X-rays. Infrared data from Webb provides views of the cloud’s regions of gas and dust. When this data is made audible, Chandra’s X-rays become high-pitched glassy tones, along with other sustained sounds to mark the appearance of extended bright sources. The clouds in Webb’s infrared data are mapped as differently pitched sounds, and stars are played as metallic plucks. There is a gap in the middle of the piece due to dark dust clouds that emit very little light.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser thatsupports HTML5 video
NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, manages the Chandra program. The Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory's Chandra X-ray Center controls science operations from Cambridge, Massachusetts, and flight operations from Burlington, Massachusetts.
The sonification program is led by the Chandra X-ray Center (CXC). The collaboration was driven by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand (CXC), Matt Russo, astrophysicist, and Andrew Santaguida, musician (SYSTEM Sounds), along with Christine Malec, consultant. More sonifications can be found atchandra.si.edu/sound.

item.title: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure
item.description:
NASA and its international partners are set to receive scientific research samples and hardware as a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft departs the International Space Station no earlier than Wednesday, Nov. 18, for its return to Earth.
Pending weather conditions, the Dragon spacecraft will undock from the Harmony module’s space-facing port at 11:05 a.m. EST, following a command sent by ground controllers at SpaceX’s facility in Hawthorne, California.
NASA’s live coverage of undocking and departure begins at 10:45 a.m., streaming through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online:
NASA and SpaceX are monitoring weather forecasts and targeting splashdown off the California coast no earlier than 1:50 a.m. Thursday, Nov. 19 (10:50 p.m. PST Nov. 18). Teams will adjust plans as needed based on splashdown conditions in the Dragon recovery area and will provide updates on splashdown timing when available. NASA will not stream the splashdown but will post updates on its space stationblog.
Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth. The returning research includes a3D-bioprinted blood vessel constructscientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth. Frozentumor organoidstreated aboard the station also will return, helping researchers identify new ways to improve cancer treatments and advance personalized medicine. Scientists will analyze frozenmicrobial samplesto better understand how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive, adapt, and evolve in space. In addition, alighting systemwill return after more than three years aboard the space station, where researchers tested its potential to support astronauts’ sleep and well-being during long-duration missions.
Filled with more than 6,300 pounds of crew supplies, science investigations, and equipment, the spacecraft arrived at the space station on Oct. 15. Itlaunchedtwo days earlier on a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for the agency’s SpaceX 35th commercial resupply services mission.
For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs, and to Mars.

item.title: NICER Status Updates
item.description:
NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations
After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.
The mission andspace stationteams are now focused on plans to finalize NICER’s 8-year archive of X-ray science observations and decommission and detach the telescope from its perch near the station’s starboard solar array.
In June 2025,NICERwas suddenly unable to swivel side-to-side beyond its current orientation, which limited its ability to track cosmic objects. The team paused data collection to investigate the issue.
Robotic cameras on the outside of the station collected photographs of NICER that helped eliminate external causes. After an extensive investigation, engineers think an internal motor has failed, limiting the telescope’s motion.
Launched in 2017, NICER embarked on an initial 18-month prime mission. Since then, it has madegroundbreaking measurementsofneutron stars, which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding ofblack holes,active galaxies, and othermysterious phenomenain our universe.
The telescope also successfullydemonstratedthe potential of pulsar-based spacecraft navigation in X-rays that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond. Closer to home, technology developed to test NICER before launch is being incorporated into prototype portableCT scanners, materials analysis systems, and other applications.
Science Observations Remain Paused for NASA’s NICER Telescope
Science operations by NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer), an X-ray telescope on the International Space Station, remain paused as the team continues to evaluate the telescope’s systems after an issue developed with one of its motors. The motor is unable to move NICER beyond its current position side to side, and the telescope’s status has not changed since operations were halted June 17.
The primary goal is to move NICER into its stowed configuration in case it needs to accommodate space station activities, though the current placement does not pose a safety issue to the station or crew. The team currently does not have a timeframe for returning to science operations.
Photos taken by robotic cameras outside the station are helping eliminate external causes for the issue. Now the team is coordinating with space station personnel to perform troubleshooting maneuvers and determine potential causes within the payload.
Since it began observing the X-ray universe in 2017, NICER has successfully demonstrated a form of deep space navigation that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond.
Designed for a prime mission of 18 months and now in its eighth year of operations, NICER has made groundbreaking measurements of neutron stars, which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding of black holes, active galaxies, and other mysterious phenomena in our universe. Technology developed to test NICER before launch is being incorporated into prototype portable CT scanners, communications systems, and several other applications on Earth for the benefit of all.
NASA’s NICER Telescope Suspends Science Operations
NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer), an X-ray telescope on the International Space Station, has paused observations due to a problem with one of the motors that drives its ability to track cosmic objects.
The NICER team paused operations June 17 when performance degradation in the motor began affecting science observations. Engineers are investigating the cause and potential solutions.
The telescope was installed near the space station’s starboard solar array in 2017. The NICER mission has successfully demonstrated a form of deep space navigation that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond. It has also made groundbreaking measurements of neutron stars, which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding of black holes, active galaxies, and other mysterious phenomena in our universe.
Following Repair, NASA’s NICER Improves Daytime Measurements
A NASA X-ray telescope on the International Space Station called NICER, or Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer, has regained additional daytime observation capabilities thanks to repairs completed during a spacewalk and a reconfiguration of its detectors.
In May 2023, NICER developed a light leak in which unwanted sunlight began entering the instrument. Photos taken from inside the space station revealed several small areas of damage to the telescope’s thin thermal shields, which block sunlight while allowing X-rays through to the detectors. Nighttime observations were unaffected, and with operational adjustments, the NICER team was able to recover about 20% of station daytime observations.

item.title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location and update the duration of the flight deployment.
A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 2. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations.
Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from crop lands and livestock farms and their interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University.
Additional low-altitude research flights with a NASA P-3 Orion aircraft are scheduled for the March to July 2027 growing season in the Midwest and California’s Central Valley with a focus on cropland.
For more information about the FarmFlux mission, visit:
https://science.nasa.gov/mission/evs-4/farm-flux/

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5072-5076: The Return of the Polygons
item.description:
Mars Science Laboratory Mission Team Members
Written by Abigail Fraeman, Deputy Project Scientist, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology
Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 13, 2026
Curiosity’s past several weeks have been very focused on drilling and analysis of the“Basque Lakes”and“Nazca”samples. We learned a lot from those drilled samples, but it’s time to hit the Martian road again and resume our climb up Mount Sharp.The Yardang uniton the upper part of the mountain is calling! As we climb higher on Mount Sharp, we’ll continue to use many of our less resource intensive science instruments like APXS, ChemCam, MAHLI, and Mastcam to document the chemistry and textures of the rocks we encounter while making purposeful upward progress. These measurements allow us to document changes in the environments that formed the rocks and that altered them over time.
The two areas we explored this week had rocks that were crisscrossed by lots of small, regular sized polygons surrounded by raised ridges. This texture was very similar tothe rocks we encountered a few months ago slightly lower on the mountain. Those unique textures really surprised us when we first saw them, and we’ve been spending time as a science team discussing how they may have formed. Polygonal textures like these can form under a variety of different conditions including shrinkage of the surface when water is lost from minerals, temperature cycling, or compaction and expansion after being buried and exposed. The data Curiosity collected this week give us more clues about the genesis of these features and what they reveal about the evolution of Mars’ habitability. We’ll also get information about the composition of the cements that form the raised ridges around the polygons.
In the orbital view of our future route, I can see the layers that we’ll reach next week or the week after have textures very similar to where we first saw the amazing field of polygons. So I’m guessing we’ll continue to encounter polygons in the next couple drives, and that they’ll look more dramatic and expansive with each drive. But this is just a guess! After over 5,000 sols of exploring with Curiosity I’ve learned Mars is full of surprises, so I’m really looking forward to seeing what’s up ahead in the new future and testing if my guess is correct.

item.title: NASA Invites Media, Public to View Roman Telescope’s First Images
item.description:
NASA will release the first images from its Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope during a live stream from the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Annual Meeting in San Francisco at 3:30 p.m. EST (12:30 p.m. PST) Monday, Dec. 7.
The images will showcase the unique scientific capabilities of Roman, which will soon capture deep, panoramic, never-before-seen views of the universe to explore the mysteries of dark energy, dark matter, and worlds outside our solar system.
Watch the unveiling on a variety of platforms online:
Roman’s first images will simultaneously post on the agency’swebsite.
The following is a list of activities for release of the first images (all times Eastern):
NASA will update this advisory later with briefing participants.
The agency also will offer embargoed interviews following the conclusion of the briefing to registered media. A recording of the media briefing will be available on the AGU website after the embargo lifts at 3:30 p.m. on Dec. 7.
NASA invites the public toclaim a corner of the universewith one of Roman’s select first images.When Roman reveals its first images, each pixel will represent a unique piece of the cosmos. Once the image is revealed, participants can look up their personal pixel and receive a digital trading card with key information they can share with NASA social accounts.
Get involved byhosting your own eventfor the reveal of Roman’s first images.
RomanlaunchedAug. 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, beginning a three-month, million-mile trip to its final orbit at the Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2. During that journey, Roman has undergone acommissioning processwhere its systems are turned on, adjusted, calibrated, and prepared to conduct science. Roman will use its large field of view and crisp infrared vision to study vast swaths of the sky and probe deeply into cosmic history. In addition to helping scientists explore dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, Roman’s surveys will support a broad range of research extending far beyond the mission’s main science goals. The mission also will feature a cutting-edge coronagraph technology demonstration to directly image planets around other stars.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is managed at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, with participation by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California; Caltech/IPAC in Pasadena, California; the Space Telescope Science Institute; and a science team comprised of scientists from various research institutions. The primary industrial partners are BAE Systems, Inc.; L3Harris Technologies; and Teledyne Scientific & Imaging.
